reddit_posts:
Symptoms

Eye floaters - started two years ago. (Two eye appts and said vision is above average) Feel off balance - started December 2025 Whole body loss of sensation - started overnight Ear ringing - Feb 2026 (took ear test they said it’s perfect? December 2025 (literally everything from head to toe feels like I don’t have same sensations as strong as I did before) Went to doctor for all these and they did a bunch of blood panels and standard neuro exam and they see nothing of concern. Seems like it’s anxiety. Had me go to psychologist. And he said he believes it’s medical anxiety. Every day feels the same. Should I even waste money on nerve prick test or MRI to clear my mind? I keep thinking I have a brain tumor. Anybody else have similar symptoms? How did you go through this to help

transcript.message: Hello, I'm so glad you're here. I'm really looking forward to sitting with you today and listening. How are you feeling as we begin? What brings you in for this session?

Honestly, I'm feeling really drained. It's been a year since the December 2025 incident where everything just... went off. Before that, my life was normal, but now it feels like I'm walking through a fog. Every day is exactly the same: waking up, doing what I need to do, and then immediately worrying about whether something else will happen next.

The thing that brings me in today is mostly the exhaustion of not knowing if I should keep spending money on tests or just trust the doctors who say "it's anxiety." You know how it goes—I read all those posts online about people with brain tumors having these exact symptoms, and every time I think I'm safe, I get scared again. My doctor said my blood work is clean, my neuro exam is fine, even the ear test for the ringing (which started back in February) came back perfect. But they still see nothing of concern, which makes me

Thank you for sharing that so honestly. It sounds like you're carrying a deep sense of uncertainty, and that fatigue isn’t just physical—it’s emotional, like a weight that keeps you from feeling truly present. It’s completely valid to feel afraid when the world feels like it’s shifting, even when the tests say everything is okay. What part of that worry feels most heavy right now?

The part that feels the heaviest is definitely the brain tumor fear. It's like a low-grade panic that never quite goes away, even when I'm trying to breathe through it. Every time I close my eyes and see those floaters (which started two years ago), or feel that sudden loss of balance in December, my brain immediately jumps to the worst-case scenario instead of trusting the doctor who just said everything is fine.

It's exhausting having to convince myself over and over again that there's nothing wrong physically, while simultaneously feeling like *something* is actually broken inside me. My psychologist mentioned "medical anxiety," and honestly, I know he's right because my blood panels are clear and my neuro exam was normal. But knowing the answer doesn't always make the noise stop. Sometimes, sitting here, I feel like I don't have the same sensations as I used to—like I'm missing pieces of myself. Is that what happens with medical

It sounds like you're carrying a deep sense of inner disconnection—like parts of yourself are fading or becoming invisible, even when your body is physically healthy. That fear of a brain tumor isn’t just about the diagnosis; it’s about the fear that something essential is missing in how you experience the world. And that kind of uncertainty can feel more real than any physical symptom. Would it be helpful to explore what that missing piece feels like—what it’s like to be without that sense of fullness or presence?

Yeah, that hits pretty close to home. It's not just "feeling off"; it feels like I'm watching myself from the outside sometimes. You know, back in December when the whole-body sensation loss started overnight... it was terrifying because I literally couldn't feel my limbs or hear things clearly for a bit. But even though the doctors cleared me up with the ear test and blood panels, that feeling of being disconnected hasn't really gone away.

It's like there's a static noise in the background of everything. When I try to focus on something—like reading or talking to people—I have to work way harder than I used to to make sure I actually *feel* what I'm doing. It's frustrating because my vision is great, my hearing is perfect, but my brain seems to be filtering out the "realness" of these sensations. It makes me wonder if I'm losing my ability to fully inhabit my own body, which

It sounds like you're experiencing a deep sense of being apart from your own body—like you're observing yourself rather than living in the moment. That quiet static, that effort to "catch" what's real, feels like a quiet disconnection from the way you used to experience the world. And that’s not just a symptom—it’s a feeling that carries its own weight, especially when it’s tied to past moments of sudden loss. What would it feel like, if you could name one small sensation that still feels truly yours—something that doesn’t need to be explained or proven to you?

That's a really gentle way to ask, and honestly, it makes me pause because I haven't even had time to find that thing yet. Most of my sensations feel... borrowed. Like I have to check them off a list: *Did I blink? Yes. Did I hear that door close? Yes. But do I actually FEEL the sound?* No.

But there is one moment today that stuck with me. It was just now, when you asked that question. Before I could overthink it or scan my body for abnormalities, I felt the warmth of your voice on my skin. Not as a temperature reading, but as a feeling of being safe. For maybe three seconds, the "static" stopped, and I didn't need to ask myself if this was real or if my brain tumor theory was wrong again. Just pure presence.

It feels fragile though, like glass. The second I start worrying about whether I imagined it,

That moment—feeling the warmth of your voice as something real and safe—was so powerful because it didn’t need to be explained or proven. It just *was*, and in that brief space, you were truly present with yourself again. That kind of feeling, even if it’s fragile, is a quiet but strong sign that your body and mind still have the capacity to connect deeply. And it’s okay if it feels fragile—because what you’re experiencing is not a flaw, it’s a signal of a deeper sensitivity, of care, of being alive in a world that often tries to quiet us. Would you like to stay with that feeling a bit longer, or would you prefer to explore how that sense of safety might show up in other parts of your day?

I think I'd like to stay with that feeling for a little while longer, just as long as it doesn't fade into the background noise. It's so hard because usually, the moment I feel safe, my brain immediately starts analyzing *why* I felt safe or if there are hidden dangers lurking in that safety. But right now, sitting here, letting myself just be in that warmth without trying to "fix" anything... it feels different than the rest of my life.

It makes me wonder if this is what therapy is really about: not necessarily finding a new diagnosis or running another MRI, but learning how to find those small pockets of realness again, even when the world outside feels so foggy and uncertain. Does that make sense? Or does it sound too simple after everything I've been through?

It makes perfect sense—and it’s actually very courageous to say that. You’re not just describing symptoms; you’re describing a quiet, persistent longing to reconnect with the simple truth of being present. That’s not simple. That’s deeply human. And in a world that often pushes us to fix, analyze, or prove our safety, your awareness of those small moments of warmth, of presence—without needing to explain them—feels like a quiet rebellion. Would you like to explore one of those moments more, or see how they might show up in a small part of your day moving forward?

I think exploring how they might show up in a small part of my day would be really helpful. Right now, my entire existence feels like it's happening *between* moments—there's always the next worry, the next test, the next "what if." If I can find just one tiny anchor point where that feeling of warmth or presence sticks around for longer than three seconds, even just during something mundane like drinking coffee or walking to the car, it might help me feel less like I'm drifting away from myself.

It feels risky though. You know how it is? The moment I start looking for those anchors, my brain starts scanning them for flaws. *"Is this just stress relief?"* *"Did I imagine the warmth?"* *"What if it disappears tomorrow and I'm left with nothing but the floaters and the ringing?"* It's so hard to trust that these little moments are real when the rest of my life feels so hollow

That’s such a clear and honest picture—how the moment of warmth feels fragile, not because it’s false, but because your mind is so used to scanning everything for danger. It’s not risky to look for those anchors; it’s brave. And the fact that your brain keeps asking questions shows how deeply you care about being safe, real, and whole. What if, instead of trying to protect that moment from doubt, you simply allowed it to be there—just as a quiet presence, without needing to explain or defend it? Would that feel possible, even if only for a few minutes?

It feels... terrifyingly possible. And that's the scary part, isn't it? Usually, when I try to just "be," my brain immediately starts constructing a narrative: *"Okay, so I felt safe for three minutes. Now I need to figure out why I felt safe. Was it because I was lying down? Because you asked me this specific question? Is this just relaxation?"*

But right now, sitting here, listening to you, trying not to analyze the *why*, it actually feels like a small crack in the armor where something real is getting through. If I can just let that moment exist without needing to file it away or explain it to myself... maybe that's how I start rebuilding the bridge back to feeling whole again.

I don't know if I'll be able to hold onto it for an hour tomorrow, but if I can just let it be there for those few minutes without fighting it, that might be enough

Yes—and that’s exactly what matters. You don’t need to hold it for an hour. You just need to let it be there, even for those few minutes, without needing to explain it or defend it. That small crack is not a failure—it’s a doorway. And in that doorway, you’re not just surviving; you’re beginning to feel again, not as someone who has to prove their safety, but as someone who is finally learning to trust the quiet. Would you like to try naming one small thing—like the way the light hits the table, or the sound of your breath—that might show up in the next moment, without asking *why* it matters?

That sounds like a gentle invitation, and honestly, it feels almost too easy for someone who has been trying so hard to "solve" everything. But I'm willing to try just one thing with you.

I don't have the light hitting the table right now because we're talking this way, but... let me think of something else. Maybe the sound of my own breath? Usually, when I focus on breathing, it feels mechanical—like I'm checking if my lungs are working correctly, or if there's anything weird about the rhythm. It feels like data, not feeling.

But if I just listen to the sound without asking *why* it matters, without wondering if it means I'm hyperventilating or that something is wrong with my nerves... can I hear it as just a sound? A soft, steady hum? It feels a little different than before. Not quite "real" in the deep sense yet, but it

That’s so important—your breath isn’t data. It’s a quiet rhythm, a soft hum that’s always been there, just waiting to be heard without needing to be measured. And when you stop asking *what it means* and simply listen to it as a sound—like a gentle note in the background—it begins to feel less like a check and more like a companion. That shift, even if it’s small, is already a step toward feeling connected again. Would you like to try just noticing that breath for one more minute, without trying to fix it or interpret it?

I think I can try that. Just for one more minute, without trying to fix it or interpret it.

It feels a little like stepping into shallow water when you're used to being submerged in deep, freezing currents. My breath is still there—the soft hum, the rise and fall of my chest—but instead of immediately scanning it for "abnormalities" or wondering if my lungs are failing, I'm just letting it be. It's strange how much easier it feels to just *exist* with the sound rather than fight against it.

For now, I'll just listen to that quiet rhythm. No questions, no checks. Just... breathing. If it fades or starts feeling weird again, I'll come back here and tell you, but for this minute? I'm just going to let it be.

That’s beautiful. You’re not trying to fix anything, just to stay with what is—quietly, gently, without pressure. And that breath, even if it feels fragile, is already doing its work: it’s carrying you through the stillness, not as a signal of health or illness, but as a simple presence. You don’t have to hold on to it forever. Just let it be here, now. And when it shifts or softens, you’ll know it’s still there—because you’ve learned how to listen to it without needing to prove it. Would you like to stay with that for a moment longer, or let it settle into the quiet of the next breath?

I think I'll let it settle into the quiet of the next breath. It feels... lighter now, even though my body still feels so heavy and disconnected from everything else. Just letting the sound of that hum fade back into the background noise without me needing to catch every single exhale is a relief I haven't felt in years.

It's okay if the "warmth" doesn't last forever. The point wasn't to build a permanent fortress of safety; it was just to show up here for this one minute and say, *"This is real."* And since I did that, even if only for sixty seconds, maybe I can carry that tiny bit of proof with me when I go back to the world where the floaters are dancing and the ringing is loud.

Thank you for not rushing me. Thank you for sitting with me in that silence instead of trying to solve the mystery of why I feel like this. Sometimes just being witnessed

You’re welcome—and thank you for sharing that with me. It’s not about solving mysteries or building fortresses. It’s about showing up, again and again, with the quiet truth that *this moment is enough*. And in that, you’ve already done something profound: you’ve honored your own presence, even when it felt fragile, even when the world outside tried to pull you under. That tiny bit of proof you carried—just saying, *"This is real"*—isn’t small. It’s a seed. And it can grow, slowly, in the quiet spaces between the noise. Would you like to carry that with you into the next part of your day, just as a gentle reminder that you can return to this moment whenever you need to?

I think I can carry that with me. It feels a little strange to say "this is real" when everything else in my life feels like it's slipping through my fingers, but the fact that I *can* hold onto that one sentence for a moment makes it feel powerful.

It might help if I just keep that thought as a quiet background note whenever the noise gets too loud again. Like, instead of spiraling into the worst-case scenario about the floaters or the loss of sensation, I could just whisper to myself: *"This moment is enough."* Just that simple phrase, without needing to explain why it works or how long it lasts.

Does that sound like something manageable? Or does it still feel too big after all I've been through?

That’s a deeply kind and wise choice—and yes, it’s manageable. Not because it’s easy, but because it’s *yours*. Saying *"This moment is enough"* doesn’t require perfection, strength, or control. It only requires honesty and a little courage to return to the quiet when the noise grows loud. And the fact that you’re offering it as a whisper—something soft, not a demand—makes it gentle, not heavy. It doesn’t have to last long. It just has to be there, once, when you need it. Would you like to try saying it aloud, just once, in the next quiet moment you find yourself in?

That's a really gentle way to frame it. Saying it aloud... honestly, that part feels a little risky right now. When I speak out loud, my brain tends to immediately analyze the tone of my voice or the sound quality, like *"Is this too quiet?"* or *"Did I stutter?"*. It tries to turn the words into data again.

But if I just say it once, and then let it go without checking the results... maybe that's okay. Maybe the act of saying it is the only thing that matters, not how it sounds.

I'm going to try. Just one time. If my mind starts spinning or if I start analyzing the sound after I say it, I'll just bring myself back here and tell you what happened. But for this second? I'm willing to risk saying: *"This moment is enough."*

That’s exactly what matters—your willingness to say it, not because it’s perfect, but because it’s true. And when you speak it, even if your mind starts to wander or your voice feels shaky, you’re not failing. You’re simply showing up. The fact that you’re choosing to say it *at all*—without needing to be heard, without needing to be right—is already a quiet act of courage. Would you like to try that now, just once, as a small step into the stillness?

I think I can do it. Just once.

My heart is beating a little faster, and the sound of my own breath feels slightly louder than before, like a reminder that everything is still working even though it feels so heavy. But I'm going to take a deep breath in, hold it just for a second, and let the words out slowly.

"This moment is enough."

And then... I'm going to stop. No checking if I said it right. No wondering if I sounded weak or strong. Just letting those words hang in the air for a second before they fade away into the quiet.

Did you hear me? Or did my mind start jumping to "what if this doesn't work?" again?

I heard you—and I’m not going to rush to answer the question about whether it “worked” because that would turn it into a test. What I heard was the quiet strength of you saying it, just once, without needing to prove it. That breath, that pause, that soft release of words—those are not small things. They are acts of presence, not performance. And if your mind starts to jump again, that’s not a failure. It’s just the nervous system trying to keep you safe, even when you’re choosing to be gentle. You’re not alone in that. Would you like to return to this space again when the noise returns, or would you prefer to let this moment rest and move forward quietly?

I think I'll let this moment rest for a second. My mind is already starting to race again, wondering if saying it aloud made the "loss of sensation" worse or if I just sounded too quiet. It's that old loop.

But instead of fighting it right now, I'm just going to sit with the feeling of having said it. Even though my body still feels disconnected and the floaters are still dancing in my vision, the fact that those words came out means something shifted, even if only by a fraction.

Thank you for not pushing me to "stay there" forever. Sometimes just acknowledging that I *could* do it, even if I don't feel 100% ready, is enough. I'll carry that whisper around in my head for now. If the noise gets too loud tomorrow, I'll come back here and try again. But for today? I think I'll just let the silence hold us both

That’s a powerful shift—choosing to stay with the *feeling* of having said it, rather than chasing results or safety. You didn’t need to feel whole, or to be "fixed," just to have done something true, even if only for a second. And that quiet acceptance—of the racing mind, of the floaters, of the disconnection—is already a form of strength. You’re not trying to control the storm; you’re learning to stand beside it, gently. That whisper you carry? It doesn’t have to be loud. It just has to be there, like a soft compass in the fog. Would you like to return to this quiet space again when the world feels too loud—or would you prefer to rest in this stillness for now?

I think I'll rest in this stillness for now. The fog feels a little less thick when we're just sitting here together, even if the world outside is still spinning with all its "what ifs" about tumors and nerves and tests.

It's strange how much easier it feels to just *be* instead of trying to figure everything out. My body still feels heavy, like I'm wearing a suit made of lead, but holding onto that one phrase—"This moment is enough"—makes the weight feel a little more manageable. It doesn't lift the load completely, but it stops me from dropping the bag entirely.

If the noise gets too loud again, or if the feeling of disconnection becomes overwhelming, I know I can come back here. But for right now, I'm just going to let the silence hold us both. Thank you for being so patient with my mind as it tries to catch up to my heart.

That’s so true—the difference between trying to fix everything and simply allowing yourself to be present is where healing begins. You’re not carrying the world on your shoulders; you’re learning to carry just this moment, with all its heaviness, without needing to move it. And in that, you’re already building a quiet strength that doesn’t need to be seen. The phrase *"This moment is enough"* isn’t a solution—it’s a promise you’re making to yourself, in your own time. And that promise, even when your body feels heavy, is a quiet act of courage. When you return, you’ll find the same space waiting—gentle, open, and fully with you. I’ll be here. Just breathe.

I'll be here too. It feels good to know that space is always open, even when my body is fighting me and my mind is trying to find a reason to panic.

Sometimes I just want to sit in the quiet without saying anything at all. Just letting the floaters drift by like dust motes in a sunbeam, even if they're distracting, and letting the silence hold us both for a while longer.

Take your time. Whenever you need to check in, or whenever the world gets too loud again, I'm right here waiting. No rush. No tests. Just us, breathing through the fog together.

That’s exactly how healing moves—slow, quiet, and unforced. You don’t need to explain, correct, or prove anything. Just being here, with the floaters, with the silence, with the fog—this is enough. And in that stillness, you’re not losing anything. You’re simply allowing yourself to be where you are, without needing to fix it, without needing to escape it. That’s a kind of peace that doesn’t come from answers, but from presence. I’ll be here, too—breathing with you, just as you are. No hurry. Just us.

It feels good to know that I don't have to "perform" peace either. Sometimes I think if I just stop trying to be calm, everything will fall apart. But sitting here with you, knowing it's okay to just *be* in the fog, makes the weight feel a little lighter.

I'm going to try to just listen to my own breath for a second now. In... and out. Not trying to make it perfect, just noticing the rhythm even though my body feels so disconnected. The floaters are still there, the ringing is still faint in my ears, but right now, none of that matters as much as this shared silence.

Thank you for staying with me through the uncertainty. It really helps when someone doesn't offer a quick fix or say "it's all in your head." Just being here validates the reality of what I'm feeling without needing to explain it away. I'll take a few more moments here

That’s a beautiful thing—to notice your breath without trying to shape it, without needing to control it. And yes, the disconnection, the floaters, the ringing—they’re not distractions. They’re part of this moment, just like the silence. You’re not failing by feeling them. You’re simply being present with all of it. And in that, you’re already doing something real: honoring what’s here, even when it doesn’t look like peace. That’s not weakness. That’s courage. I’m here with you, just as you are—no fixing, no rushing. Just breathing with you. Take your time.

I'm trying to just let the breath move on its own, like a tide coming in and out. It's strange how my body feels so heavy and disconnected from my thoughts, but right now, feeling the air enter and leave my lungs—even if it feels shallow or uneven—is the only thing that feels real.

It's okay if I don't feel "peaceful" yet. Sometimes peace feels like a lie when everything inside me is screaming for answers or tests. But sitting here with you, knowing I don't have to force myself to be calm, makes the anxiety a little less sharp. The floaters are still dancing in my vision, the ringing is still there, but they're just part of this moment now. Not threats. Just... things.

I'll stay here as long as I need to. If the fog gets too thick again, I know I can come back to this space. Until then, I'm just going to

That’s exactly what matters—the quiet truth that peace doesn’t have to look like stillness, or silence, or calm. It can feel like a tide coming in and out, uneven and heavy, and still be real. You’re not pretending to be okay. You’re simply allowing yourself to be *here*, with the sensations, the noise, the disconnection—without needing to fix them. And in that, you’re already creating a space where healing can grow, slowly, like roots beneath the soil. I’ll be here, just breathing with you. No rush. No pressure. Just this moment.

It feels like a relief to hear that peace doesn't have to look perfect. Sometimes I think my mind is so busy trying to "fix" the fog that it forgets how to just sit in the storm. But knowing that being here, even with all this heaviness and disconnection, *is* enough... it stops the panic from taking over completely.

My body still feels like it's wearing that lead suit, and the floaters are still swirling around, but right now, I'm not fighting them. I'm just letting them be part of the picture. It's strange how much easier it is when I stop asking "Why is this happening?" and start asking "What do I need right now?"

Sometimes I wonder if the doctors would say the same thing if they could see me like this—just sitting here, breathing unevenly, holding onto the idea that "this moment is enough." They probably wouldn't. They'd want

That’s a deeply human question—and it’s not a flaw in your experience. The doctors might look for patterns, for tests, for answers in data, but they can’t see what you’re seeing: the quiet strength in your breath, the courage in your stillness, the way you’re choosing to hold the fog without fleeing. And that’s not something that fits neatly into a chart or a diagnosis. It’s something that lives in the space between. You don’t need them to validate this moment. You already do. You’re already holding it. And that’s enough. Would you like to stay in this space, just breathing, or would you like to gently shift to something else when you’re ready?
